newsitem.title: USA: Mass. lawmakers take up bill restricting Keno.
newsitem.headline: Mass. lawmakers take up bill restricting Keno.

text.p: Legislation to restrict the growth of the Massachusetts Lottery Commission's most popular game was unveiled Tuesday by lawmakers, who also want greater oversight of efforts to promote and sell all of the lottery's games, State House News reported.
The bill, now headed to the House Ways and Means Committee, was crafted by the House and Senate chairmen of the Government Regulations Committee and endorsed by the full committee.
For the past two years, concern has grown over the increasing number of establishments being licensed to offer customers Keno, a fast-paced and addictive electronic game.

The game was authorized in 1994 with the intention that it would be played in bars and restaurants. Since then, the number of Keno licenses has skyrocketed and there is concern in many communities that its presence in convenience stores preys on neighborhood youngsters, and those who can least afford to gamble.

The new bill would cap the number of Keno licenses the SLC can issue at 1,650, and eventually restrict the game to "alcohol-pouring establishments", such as bars, taverns and restaurants. The game would be phased out of convenience stores over the next 10 years.

Beginning July 1, new Keno licenses can only be issued to bars and restaurants. If a convenience store is sold or goes out of business, its license would be returned to the State Lottery Commission, under the terms of the bill.
By July 1, 2007, Keno would not be played in any convenience stores.

Only those 21 or older could play the electronic game under the new bill. The legal age for buying tickets is now 18, and the change would match the legal gambling age to that at which a person can be served alcohol in a bar or restaurant.

Other initiatives in the bill require that a hotline number for compulsive gamblers be flashed across the screen between Keno games; provide that no Keno licenses be issued to establishments within 200 feet of any school, check-cashing or pawnbroker business; impose penalties for violating new restrictions; and allow vendors to appeal any violation other than non-payment.
A seven-member lottery sales agent advisory board would be established under the bill to oversee and review SLC policies.
